title: Cognitive Dissonance Dominates Hormuz
gist: Despite Trump's repeated claims that the Strait of Hormuz is fully demined and open, shipping traffic has stayed near 30 transits/day versus a pre-war average of 129, with most vessels avoiding the official shipping lane — evidence the market trusts on-the-ground reality over presidential statements, a pattern the author says is also visible in Greenland and Iran-regime-collapse claims and is corroding U.S. credibility broadly.

themes.theme: The market is ignoring Trump's Hormuz claims

insights.claim: Despite Trump declaring on Aug. 25 and again on Aug. 27 ('That sucker is open') that all mines were cleared from the Strait of Hormuz's Traffic Separation Scheme, ship traffic through the strait remained at roughly 30 transits per day, versus a pre-war daily average of 129, with most ships routing along Iranian and Omani coastlines rather than the supposedly cleared official lane.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Shipping-traffic data is a real-time, hard-to-fake proxy for the credibility of official war-zone safety claims; the persistent ~75% shortfall versus pre-war transit volume signals the market still prices meaningful mine/attack risk in Hormuz despite official reassurance, a leading indicator for tanker rates and oil-supply risk premia.
insights.quote: ship traffic remained steady at around 30 transits each day, compared to a daily average of 129 before the war
insights.locator: The shipping community, alas, didn't believe the announcement

insights.claim: U.S. Centcom leader Brad Cooper's public statement was more precise than Trump's: he said mines were cleared from 'internationally recognized transit routes' rather than claiming all mines everywhere were gone, since it's impossible to know how many mines Iran laid or exactly where.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: The gap between the president's absolute claims and his own military commander's hedged language is itself a signal of unreliable top-line White House messaging on war-zone conditions relevant to shippers and insurers.
insights.quote: internationally recognized transit routes are free of Iranian sea mines thanks to the incredible work of the U.S. military.
insights.locator: The following day, U.S. Central Command leader Brad Cooper

insights.claim: On Aug. 30 the U.S. fired missiles and rockets at Iran after Centcom discovered Iran was planning to lay more mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and the next day Trump posted an AI-generated video depicting Iran's Kharg Island 'being blown to smithereens,' after which oil prices rose.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Direct causal link between an AI-generated presidential social media post depicting an attack on a key Iranian oil export terminal (Kharg Island) and an oil price move — a concrete example of information-warfare/social-media content now functioning as a market-moving catalyst.
insights.locator: Trump posted an artificial intelligence video

themes.theme: A recurring pattern of presidential claims diverging from reality

insights.claim: The author frames 'cognitive dissonance' as a recurring pattern in Trump's foreign policy: claiming Greenlanders 'want to be with us' despite 85% opposing U.S. annexation in a prior poll, promising Iranians the 'hour of your freedom is at hand' with no U.S. intelligence indicating the Iranian regime would collapse, and declaring Hormuz fully open contrary to shipping data.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Provides a reusable pattern-recognition framework — presidential claims about foreign-policy 'facts on the ground' (territorial sentiment, regime stability, war-zone safety) should be checked against independent data (polling, intelligence assessments, traffic/shipping data) rather than taken at face value when pricing related geopolitical risk.
insights.quote: cognitive dissonance now seems to dominate Trump's relations with the world.
insights.locator: Indeed, cognitive dissonance now dominates the Strait of Hormuz

insights.claim: U.S. intelligence agencies had no information indicating the Iranian regime would collapse or fold in the event of a U.S. attack, contradicting Trump's public messaging to the Iranian people that 'the hour of your freedom is at hand.'
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Confirms a specific instance where presidential rhetoric ran directly counter to the U.S. intelligence community's own assessment — a warning sign for over-reading administration statements as reflecting actual government analysis on Iran regime stability.
insights.quote: U.S. intelligence agencies, though, had no information indicating that the Iranian regime would collapse or fold in case of a U.S. attack.
insights.locator: U.S. intelligence agencies, though, had no information

insights.claim: The author argues cognitive dissonance can work temporarily for a powerful autocratic-leaning leader (citing Trump's belief that Kim Jong Un was his 'friend,' which Kim reciprocated superficially for North Korea's benefit) but eventually 'reality proves stubborn,' and each unfounded claim (Hormuz demined, Greenlander sentiment, Iran regime collapse) gets disproven by verifiable facts.
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: Suggests a bounded shelf-life for policy built on unverified presidential claims — useful as a heuristic for discounting the durability of any Trump administration position that lacks independent corroboration.
insights.quote: For a certain amount of time, cognitive dissonance works—if one is a powerful country ruled by a person with autocratic tendencies... But at a certain point, reality proves stubborn.
insights.locator: For a certain amount of time, cognitive dissonance works

themes.theme: Eroding U.S. credibility as a second-order cost

insights.claim: The author claims that people seeking facts about matters involving the United States increasingly consult sources other than the U.S. government, going so far as to say 'even Iranian and Russian government reports seem to hew closer to the facts than Trump's posts do.'
insights.speaker: Elisabeth Braw
insights.so_what: A striking, explicitly stated claim that adversary-state media is now viewed as more reliable than official U.S. statements — an extreme marker of eroded U.S. informational credibility with implications for how allies and markets weight official U.S. communications on conflicts.
insights.quote: Even Iranian and Russian government reports seem to hew closer to the facts than Trump's posts do.
insights.locator: Whatever marginal gains that Trump may achieve
